Water keeps plant cells firm and supports photosynthesis. Without it, leaves droop and life processes slow or stop.
Wilting is an early water-stress sign.
Different plants tolerate drought differently.
What happens to blood when it travels through the lungs?
It picks up oxygen and drops off carbon dioxide.
It turns into stomach acid.
It stores leftover bones.
It becomes plant sap.
In the lungs, gas exchange occurs. Blood gains oxygen for the body and releases carbon dioxide to be exhaled.
The heart sends blood to the lungs and body.
Oxygen-rich blood fuels active cells.
What do the kidneys help do?
Pump air into the ears
Digest food using chlorophyll
Grow new skull bones each hour
Kidneys clean the blood by removing wastes and extra water. The wastes leave the body as urine.
Healthy kidneys support internal balance.
Drinking enough water helps body systems, including the kidneys.
Why must the heart keep beating?
It must keep moving blood that carries oxygen and nutrients to body cells.
It only beats to make musical sounds.
It beats to cool the room temperature.
It beats so hair can photosynthesize.
Cells need a constant supply of oxygen and nutrients. If blood stops moving, tissues cannot work for long.
The heart is a lifelong pump.
Circulation links lungs, digestive nutrients, and body cells.
During hard exercise, why might muscles feel tired?
They are using energy quickly and may not get oxygen fast enough for a while.
They have turned into cartilage permanently.
They no longer connect to bones.
They are allergic to breathing.
Active muscles demand lots of energy and oxygen. When demand is high, fatigue builds until you rest and recover.
Blood delivery and breathing support muscles.
Rest helps muscles recover after activity.
What do nerves do in the body?
They carry messages between the brain, spinal cord, and body parts.
They digest vitamins in the stomach only.
They store fat for plant growth.
They replace blood vessels completely.
Nerves are like communication lines. They let you sense the world and control movement and many automatic body functions.
The nervous system coordinates the body.
Signals travel quickly along nerves.
What does a thermometer measure?
Temperature
Length only
Loudness of music only
The number of leaves on a tree
Thermometers show how hot or cold something is. Scientists use them when temperature matters in a test.
Choose tools that match the question.
Record temperature with correct units, like °F or °C.
Why should a science log include the date?
Dates help you track when observations were made and compare changes over time.
Dates make plants grow faster by themselves.
Dates replace the need for measurements.
Dates erase experimental errors.
Time stamps keep records organized. You can see growth, weather links, or which trial came first.
Clear notebooks support good science.
Details make data useful later.
If you test how water affects seed growth, what should you change?
The amount of water, while keeping other conditions the same
Water, light, soil type, and temperature all at once
Only the color of your notebook
Nothing at all, and still claim a fair test
To learn about water's effect, water should be the main changed variable. Keep light, soil, and temperature steady for fairness.
One main variable makes results clearer.
Controls and constants support fair comparisons.
What is a safe practice near hot equipment in a science activity?
Use care, follow adult directions, and never touch hot surfaces.
Grab hot glassware with bare hands to test heat.
Lean over boiling liquids without attention.
Ignore warning signs about heat.
Heat can burn skin quickly. Teachers set rules—like using tongs and waiting for cooling—to prevent injuries.
Heat safety is part of lab responsibility.
Ask before handling warm materials.
Which sentence is written like a hypothesis?
If a plant gets more light, then it will grow taller.
Science is fun sometimes.
I like blue notebooks.
Today is Tuesday.
A hypothesis often uses an if-then idea you can test. It predicts a relationship you can check with evidence.
Hypotheses should be testable.
Results may support or not support a hypothesis.
Why do scientists compare results from different trials or groups?
Comparing helps them see differences and decide what the evidence shows.
Comparing deletes the need for any hypothesis.
Comparing means changing every variable randomly.
Comparing forbids using tables or graphs.
Comparison is how patterns appear. Side-by-side results show whether a change made a real difference.
Evidence becomes clearer with comparison.
Fair groups make comparisons meaningful.
What is a controlled variable (constant) in an experiment?
A condition you keep the same on purpose
The only thing you change every minute
A guess you never write down
A broken tool you still use
Constants stay steady so they do not confuse the results. For example, same soil type while testing water amount.
Identify change, measure, and keep-the-same factors.
Controls and constants improve fairness.
What does it mean to replicate an experiment?
Do it again to see if you get similar results
Invent new numbers without testing
Change the question after seeing the answer
Hide the method from everyone
Replication checks reliability. If others—or you—can repeat the method and find similar results, confidence grows.
Science values results that can be repeated.
Clear methods make replication possible.
What can reduce measurement error?
Using tools correctly and measuring more than once
Estimating wildly without looking
Rounding to whatever looks nicest
Switching units mid-table without noting it
Careful technique and repeats lower mistakes. Knowing a tool's limits also helps you interpret data wisely.
All measurements have some uncertainty.
Good habits improve data quality.
You measure plant growth as 4 without units. What is the problem?
Without units, nobody knows if you mean 4 centimeters, 4 inches, or something else.
Numbers never need labels in science.
Units only matter for temperature.
Four is not allowed in data tables.
Units give numbers meaning. Clear labels prevent confusion when sharing or graphing results.
Always include units with measurements.
Convert carefully if you change unit systems.
A student's conclusion disagrees with all of the data. What should they do?
Revise the conclusion so it fits the evidence.
Erase the data and keep the conclusion.
Ignore the mismatch completely.
Add made-up points until it matches.
In science, evidence leads. If data do not support a claim, the claim should change—or more testing may be needed.
Honesty about results matters.
Surprising data can still be valuable.
What is a control group used for?
It provides a baseline to compare with the group that received the change.
It is the group allowed to break safety rules.
It is a group that skips all measurements.
It is a group that changes every variable.
The control group does not get the experimental treatment. Differences from the test group help show the treatment's effect.
Comparison needs a baseline.
Control groups strengthen fair tests.
Which trait fits mammals?
They have hair or fur and feed milk to their babies.
They all breathe with gills underwater only.
They all lay hard-shelled eggs in nests like birds do exclusively.
They make food from sunlight using leaves.
Mammals are a group of animals with shared traits, including fur/hair and milk for young. Dogs, cats, and humans are mammals.
Classification groups living things by shared features.
Not all mammals look alike, but they share key traits.
Cows are best described as which kind of eater?
Herbivores that eat plants
Carnivores that eat only meat
Animals that eat only rocks
Animals that do not need food
Cows graze on grass and other plants. Their digestive systems are adapted for a plant-based diet.
Herbivores, carnivores, and omnivores have different diets.
Teeth and digestion often match diet type.
Why must animals living on land still get water?
Their body processes need water to keep working.
Water is only for fish and never for land animals.
Land animals drink water only to change color.
Water replaces oxygen for land animals.
Water is essential for life on land and in water. Animals drink or get moisture from food and habitats.
All animals need water somehow.
Dry habitats make water especially precious.
What do bees collect from flowers?
Nectar (and they also pick up pollen)
Only bird feathers
Only fish scales
Only tree bark for nests in oceans
Bees visit flowers for nectar to make food. While doing so, they often move pollen between flowers.
Flower visits can help both bees and plants.
Pollination supports seed and fruit production.
What covering do birds have that helps with flight and warmth?
Feathers
Wet fish scales only
Thick tree bark
Plastic shells
Feathers are a key bird trait. They help with flying, steering, and keeping warm.
Birds are the only living animals with feathers.
Different feathers have different jobs.
Which animals use gills to get oxygen from water?
Most fish
Dogs
Eagles
House cats
Gills are specialized for underwater gas exchange. Land pets like dogs and cats use lungs instead.
Breathing structures match habitats.
Oxygen is needed whether it comes from air or water.
What is one adaptation that helps animals survive cold climates?
Thick fur, fat layers, or behaviors that conserve heat
Losing all body covering in winter
Standing in wind with wet skin on purpose all night
Stopping food intake for months without any stores
Insulation and smart behaviors reduce heat loss. Some animals also hibernate or migrate.
Adaptations solve environmental challenges.
Cold places select for heat-saving traits.
What does a food web show?
Many linked feeding relationships in an ecosystem
Only the weather forecast
A list of classroom rules
The planets in order from the sun
Food webs are more complete than single chains. They show how energy connects many plants and animals.
